facts.statement: Cycnorhamphus is a genus of gallodactylid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic of France and Germany, approximately 152 million years old.
facts.quote: Cycnorhamphus (meaning "swan beak") is a genus of gallodactylid ctenochasmatoid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic period of France and Germany, about 152 million years ago.

facts.statement: The type species was originally named Pterodactylus suevicus by Friedrich August Quenstedt in 1855 based on a fossil found near Nusplingen in Württemberg.
facts.quote: In 1855, a fossil in a plate of shale from the Kimmeridgian, found near Nusplingen in Württemberg, holotype GPIT "Orig. Quenstedt 1855, Taf. 1" or GPIT 80, was named Pterodactylus suevicus by Friedrich August Quenstedt.

facts.statement: Harry Govier Seeley established the genus Cycnorhamphus in 1870 by reassigning Pterodactylus suevicus to it.
facts.quote: In 1870, Harry Govier Seeley assigned P. suevicus to a new genus: Cycnorhamphus.

facts.statement: The genus name Cycnorhamphus is derived from Greek words meaning "swan" and "beak", referencing the animal's snout shape.
facts.quote: The name is derived from Greek κύκνος, kyknos, "swan" and ράμφος, ramphos, "beak", in reference to the snout shape.

facts.statement: Felix Plieninger rejected the separation of Pterodactylus and Cycnorhamphus in 1907, a view held by most paleontologists for over sixty years.
facts.quote: In 1907 however, Felix Plieninger rejected the split between Pterodactylus and Cycnorhamphus and denied the validity of C. fraasii.

facts.statement: Jacques Fabre named the species Gallodactylus canjuersensis in 1974 based on a specimen found in the Les Besson quarries near Aiguines, France.
facts.quote: In 1974, French paleontologist Jacques Fabre based on this specimen, MNHN CNJ-71, named a new species Gallodactylus canjuersensis.

facts.statement: Christopher Bennett argued in 1996 that Cycnorhamphus has priority over Gallodactylus, renaming the French species Cycnorhamphus canjuersensis.
facts.quote: However, in 1996, Christopher Bennett pointed out that such mistakes do not invalidate a name and that therefore Cycnorhamphus has priority, making Gallodactylus canjuersensis C. canjuersensis.

facts.statement: Christopher Bennett formally synonymized Cycnorhamphus canjuersensis and Cycnorhamphus suevicus in 2010 and 2012, suggesting differences were due to age, sex, or individual variation.
facts.quote: In 2010 and 2012, Bennett published further re-studies of the fossils, concluding that the differences between the two species could be explained by age, sex or individual variation, and formally synonymized C. canjuersensis and C. suevicus.

facts.statement: Cycnorhamphus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 152.21 and 145.06 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (152.21 to 145.06 million years ago)

facts.statement: Recent studies of a specimen nicknamed "The Painten Pelican" reveal that Cycnorhamphus had unusual peg-like teeth at the jaw tips that became blunter and stouter in older individuals.
facts.quote: recent work on a specimen nicknamed "The Painten Pelican" has revealed that the animal possesses a very unusual jaw anatomy, with peg-like teeth at the jaw tips - blunter and stouter in older individuals -

facts.statement: The jaw anatomy includes curvatures forming an opening behind the teeth, occupied by two mineralized soft tissue structures from the upper jaw.
facts.quote: jaw curvatures behind said teeth that form angled arcs away from the biting surface, forming thus an opening, and two poorly understood soft tissue structures occupying this opening from the upper jaw, showing mineralization.

facts.statement: Researchers speculate that Cycnorhamphus used its unique jaws to crush or bisect hard invertebrates like mollusks, similar to openbill storks.
facts.quote: It has been speculated that the jaws functioned similar to those of openbill storks, allowing the animal to hold hard invertebrates like mollusks and either crush or bisect them.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Cycnorhamphus within the family Gallodactylidae, as the sister taxon to Normannognathus.
facts.quote: They placed the Cycnorhamphus within the clade Euctenochasmatia, more precisely within the family Gallodactylidae, sister taxon to Normannognathus.

facts.statement: Cycnorhamphus had a wingspan of approximately 135 centimeters.
facts.quote: Su envergadura era de cerca de 135 centímetros.

facts.statement: Cycnorhamphus had a unique beak shape that curved both upward and downward compared to other pterosaurs.
facts.quote: El hocico de Cycnorhampus era diferente al de otros pterosaurios, ya que estaba curvado hacia arriba y hacia abajo
